title: Introduction to R
text:
R programming language
R first appeared in 1993 and is a programming language designed for working with data and statistics.
R is usually interpreted: you write commands and R runs them directly, without a separate compile step.
For example, ask R to do a calculation:

2 + 2

[1] 4

title: Introduction to R
text:
Functions in R
You can define functions in R like:

sumFun <- function(a, b) {
  a + b
}

And use them later as:

sumFun(5, 6)

[1] 11

title: Introduction to R
text:
Packages in R
Packages are collections of functions and other tools that people develop and share for you to use.
Many R packages are distributed through CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network), a collection of servers that hosts R packages and checks submitted updates. Package authors maintain their packages; CRAN helps make them available to the R community.

To install a package you can just type:

install.packages("tibble")
# or, if you have pak installed
pak::pkg_install("tibble")



You can either call a function using :::

tibble::tibble(a = 1)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
      a
  <dbl>
1     1




Or using library(), which makes the package’s functions available:

library(tibble)
tibble(a = 1)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
      a
  <dbl>
1     1




In general we will use the latter option (library()).

title: Introduction to R
text:
The pipe operator |>

The pipe operator was introduced in R 4.1 and it is widely used in R. It concatenates the use of two functions, for example:

library(dplyr)

x <- tibble(a = 1)
x

# A tibble: 1 × 1
      a
  <dbl>
1     1

x <- mutate(x, b = 1)
x

# A tibble: 1 × 2
      a     b
  <dbl> <dbl>
1     1     1



You can simplify this code with:

x <- tibble(a = 1) |>
  mutate(b = 1)

title: Introduction to R
text:
Meet the tidyverse
The tidyverse is a collection of R packages that work well together for common data tasks.


dplyr: wrangle data (filter, select, create columns, summarise)

ggplot2: make plots

readr and tidyr: read and reshape data
plus packages for strings, factors, iteration, and more

title: Introduction to R
section: Some examples: a consistent way to work with data
text:
Some examples: a consistent way to work with data
Tidyverse functions use a consistent style: give a data frame to a function, and get a data frame back.

library(tibble)

people <- tibble(
  name = c("Alex", "Sam", "Jo"),
  age = c(24, 31, 19),
  group = c("A", "B", "A")
)

people

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  name    age group
  <chr> <dbl> <chr>
1 Alex     24 A    
2 Sam      31 B    
3 Jo       19 A    


tibble() is the tidyverse’s friendly take on a data frame. It prints a quick preview and keeps the data in a familiar rectangular format.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Read, transform, and summarise
Use |> to read a data workflow from top to bottom. Here we keep adults, add a column, and count people in each group:

library(dplyr)
people |>
  filter(age >= 18) |>
  mutate(age_next_year = age + 1) |>
  count(group)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  group     n
  <chr> <int>
1 A         2
2 B         1



Some handy dplyr verbs:


filter() keeps rows

select() keeps columns

mutate() creates or changes columns

summarise() calculates a summary

arrange() sorts rows

title: Introduction to R
text:
What is an R Project?
An R Project is a folder for one piece of work, with a small .Rproj file that lets RStudio recognise and reopen it.

Keep your scripts, notes, data, and results together
RStudio opens the project folder as the working directory
Use paths relative to the project, so your code is easier to share and rerun

Think of it as a tidy home for an analysis. One project per workshop or analysis is a good place to start.

title: Introduction to R
text:
A simple project layout
There is no single right layout. Start small and add folders when you need them:
my-analysis/
├── my-analysis.Rproj
├── R/                 # scripts and functions
├── data/              # input data (keep originals unchanged)
└── Results/           # tables, plots, and other outputs
RStudio creates the .Rproj file for you. You create the folders that make sense for your work.

title: Introduction to R
section: Let’s create your first R Project
text:
Let’s create your first R Project
In RStudio:

Choose File → New Project…

Choose New Directory, then New Project

Give it a name, for example r-introduction, and choose where to save it
Select Create Project


You should now see the project name in the top-right of RStudio. Save this presentation’s practice script inside the project, then make folders such as data and Results if you need them.

title: Introduction to R
section: Find the project root with here
text:
Find the project root with here


library(here)
here()

[1] "/home/runner/work/HDS-OMOP-course/HDS-OMOP-course"




dir.create(here("Results"))

That creates a Results folder in the project root. You can use the same idea to read or save files inside the project.

We should always work within an R Project for each analysis.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
CodelistGenerator

The CodelistGenerator R package provides tools to


Explore OMOP CDM vocabularies available in the database
Generate codelists systematically using vocabulary-based search strategies
Generate codelist diagnostics to assess code use and identify potentially missing concepts

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Generating candidate concepts
Today, we’ll focus on the getCandidateCodes() function to identify candidate concepts for our two phenotypes.

getCandidateCodes(
  cdm,
  keywords,
  exclude = NULL,
  domains = "Condition",
  vocabularyId = NULL,
  standardConcept = "Standard",
  searchInSynonyms = FALSE,
  searchNonStandard = FALSE,
  includeDescendants = TRUE,
  includeAncestor = FALSE
)


The function returns candidate concepts for review, together with the search strategy used to identify them.
This allows us to define a systematic and reproducible codelist search strategy.

Note

Before cohort construction, this preliminary codelist is clinically reviewed.

text:
CohortConstructor

CohortConstructor provides tools to create and manipulate cohorts using the OMOP CDM.

Create base cohorts from codelists
Apply demographic and observation requirements

Apply additional clinical requirements

Define cohort entry and exit


Combine, collapse, and manipulate cohort records

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Primary hypertension cohort

We will progressively apply our cohort inclusion criteria to identify adults with primary (essential) hypertension.

Create a base cohort from our essential hypertension codelist
Require ≥ 180 days of prior observation

Restrict to age ≥ 18 years

Require a second hypertension record within 365 days

Exit at end of observation

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Primary hypertension cohort
→ Create the base cohort
We first create a base cohort from condition records corresponding to concepts in our preliminary hypertension codelist:

hypertensionCodelist <- list("essential_hypertension" = hypertensionCodes$concept_id)

cdm$essential_hypertension_base <- conceptCohort(
  cdm = cdm,
  conceptSet = hypertensionCodelist,
  name = "essential_hypertension_base"
)


At this stage, each qualifying hypertension record can contribute to cohort entry.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Primary hypertension cohort
→ Apply the inclusion criteria
Now we apply inclusion criteria in a pipeline-fashion to refine the base cohort:

cdm$essential_hypertension <- cdm$essential_hypertension_base |>

  # Age ≥18 and ≥180 days of prior observation
  requireDemographics(
    ageRange = c(18, 150),
    minPriorObservation = 180,
    name = "essential_hypertension"
  ) |>

  # Require another hypertension record within 365 days
  requireCohortIntersect(
    targetCohortTable = "essential_hypertension_base",
    window = c(1, 365),
    intersections = c(1, Inf),
    name = "essential_hypertension"
  ) |>

  # Follow until the end of observation
  exitAtObservationEnd(
    name = "essential_hypertension"
  )

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
More complex phenotype definitions
Our primary hypertension cohort was a simple example to illustrate the workflow.
We can also implement more complex phenotype definitions combining different types of clinical evidence.

For instance we could use systolic and diastolic blood pressure measurements:

cdm$systolic_blood_pressure <- measurementCohort(
  cdm = cdm, 
  conceptSet = codelist["systolic_blood_pressure"],
  valueAsNumber = list(c(140, 99999)),
  name = "systolic_blood_pressure"
)

cdm$diastolic_blood_pressure <- measurementCohort(
  cdm = cdm, 
  conceptSet = codelist["diastolic_blood_pressure"],
  valueAsNumber = list(c(90, 99999)),
  name = "diastolic_blood_pressure"
)

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Warfarin cohort
→ Create treatment episodes and identify new users
We now combine nearby exposures into treatment episodes and apply our new-user criteria:

cdm$warfarin_new_users <- cdm$warfarin_base |>

  # Collapse exposures separated by ≤30 days
  collapseCohorts(
    gap = 30,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  ) |>

  # Require ≥365 days of prior observation
  requireDemographics(
    minPriorObservation = 365,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  ) |>

  # No warfarin exposure during the previous 365 days
  requireCohortIntersect(
    targetCohortTable = "warfarin_base",
    window = c(-365, -1),
    intersections = 0,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  )

PhenotypeR
PhenotypeR provides a standardised set of diagnostics to review and evaluate phenotypes created using the OMOP CDM.







Database diagnostics

databaseDiagnostics()








Codelist diagnostics

codelistDiagnostics()






Cohort diagnostics

cohortDiagnostics()








Population diagnostics

populationDiagnostics()

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Database Diagnostics
Summarise the database metadata including:

Snapshot
Summary of the person table

Summary of the observation period

Summary of the clinical tables (e.g., condition_occurrence) where concepts from the codelists defining the cohorts are found.









Note








Database diagnostics use functionality from OmopSketch.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Codelist Diagnostics

Summarise the codelist associated with your cohort including:


Achilles codes use (only if ACHILLES tables are present)

Orphan codes use (only if ACHILLES tables are present)
Cohort code use

Measurement code use (only if measurement concepts are present in your codelist)

Drug diagnostics (only if drug concepts are present in your codelist)










Note








Codelist diagnostics use functionality from CodelistGenerator to evaluate the use of concepts from our codelists in the OMOP CDM.
If the codelists contain measurement concepts, MeasurementDiagnostics is used to evaluate those concepts.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text: Cohort Diagnostics

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Cohort Diagnostics
Summarise and evaluate the cohorts including:

Cohort count & attrition

Cohort characteristics — Baseline characteristics of the cohort

Large-scale characteristics — Clinical records observed in different time windows

Compare cohorts — Overlap and timing between cohorts (if multiple cohorts)


Cohort survival — Survival until death (if death table is available)










Note








Cohort diagnostics use functionality from CohortCharacteristics to characterise and compare cohorts, and CohortSurvival to perform survival analyses.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Population Diagnostics

Contextualises the frequency of your study cohorts in the database calculating:

Incidence
Period Prevalence










Note








Population diagnostics use functionality from IncidencePrevalence to estimate the incidence and prevalence of our cohorts in the database population.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Run diagnostics together
Rather than running each diagnostic separately, phenotypeDiagnostics() allows us to run them together.

result <- phenotypeDiagnostics(
  cohort,
  databaseDiagnostics = list(),
  codelistDiagnostics = list(),
  cohortDiagnostics = list(),
  populationDiagnostics = list()
)


We can choose which diagnostics to run and customise their parameters.

result <- phenotypeDiagnostics(
  cohort,
  databaseDiagnostics = list(),
  codelistDiagnostics = list(),
  cohortDiagnostics = list(
    cohortSample = 1000
  ),
  populationDiagnostics = NULL
)

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
section: Run diagnostics of hypertension and warfarin cohorts together
text:
Run diagnostics of hypertension and warfarin cohorts together
We created our two cohort separately. To run phenotyper, we can bring them together into a single cohort table and then run PhenotypeR functions to this table.

cdm <- bind(
  cdm$essential_hypertension,
  cdm$warfarin_new_users,
  name = "phenotypes"
)
cdm$phenotypes |> settings()

1                    1 essential_hyper… 5.4         v5.0 29-APR-16     18_150

Run phenotype diagnostics

Now we can evaluate both phenotypes using the same standardised diagnostic workflow.

result <- phenotypeDiagnostics(cohort = cdm$phenotypes)



Then we can use the function shinyDiagnostics to create a shinyApp to review results:



shinyDiagnostics(result = result, directory = here())

Let’s get started
Does everyone have a GitHub username?

Share your GitHub username please :)

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
section: Git vs GitHub vs GitHub Desktop
text:
Git vs GitHub vs GitHub Desktop

Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes in source code during software development and allows multiple developers to collaborate efficiently.


GitHub is a web-based platform that provides hosting for Git repositories, along with collaborative features like issue tracking, pull requests, and project management.


GitHub Desktop is a graphical user interface (GUI) application that simplifies the interaction with Git and GitHub, allowing users to perform common repository operations without using the command line.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Repository (Repo)
A repository is essentially a project’s folder. It contains all the project files, including code, documentation, images, and, most importantly, the entire history of every change made to those files.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Explore repository
https://github.com/oxford-pharmacoepi/Tidy-R-programming-with-OMOP

A README.md is a useful front page for a repository. It can include:

A summary of the repository.
Instructions for installing a package, running code, or using a tool.
An overview of the repository folders.
How to contribute.
License information.
Acknowledgments.
Contact details.
Citation information.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Formatting Markdown files
You can use Markdown syntax to format a text file:

# to add a heading.
--- on its own line to add a horizontal rule.
- for bullet points.
*text* for italic text.
**text** for bold text.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
section: YOUR TURN Let’s create a repo in oxford-pharmacoepi
text:
YOUR TURN Let’s create a repo in oxford-pharmacoepi

In GitHub Desktop, choose File → New Repository…
Give the repository a name, choose where to save it, and click Create Repository.

The repository now exists on your computer only.

Click Publish repository. In the dialog, choose oxford-pharmacoepi from the organization menu, then click Publish Repository.

You now have a repository on GitHub. Open it on the website and have a look around.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
YOUR TURN Download the codelist
Now go to the Downloads section of the course website and look for your username.

Download the codelist assigned to you.
Add it to the folder of your repo
Let’s see the changes

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Commit
A commit is a snapshot of your repository at a specific point in time. Commits are the building blocks of Git history.

Every commit has a unique ID (SHA), an author, a timestamp, and a commit message that explains why the change was made.
Commits are created locally with Git.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
section: YOUR TURN Create a commit with the codelist
text:
YOUR TURN Create a commit with the codelist

Add a message and click commit.
The commit is still local. It will appear on GitHub after you push it.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Push & Pull
These are the actions used to synchronise your local Git repository with the remote repository on GitHub:

Push: Send your committed changes from your computer to the remote repository on GitHub.
Pull: Fetch changes from GitHub and integrate them into your current local branch. We will practise this later.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
YOUR TURN Push to GitHub

Push your changes to GitHub
Now you should see that the codelist appears in the GitHub website

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Issues

An issue is a place to track a task, bug, or idea. It gives the team a place to discuss the work, assign responsibility, and keep track of progress.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Issues

Labels: Labels are tags used to categorise and organise issues by topic, priority, or status.
Assignee: The assignee is the person responsible for handling or resolving the issue.
Type: The type describes the issue, for example a bug, feature request, or task.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
YOUR TURN Open an issue

Open an issue in your repo (you need to do that from the GitHub website)
Ask a colleague to review your codelist. The Downloads page lists who you should ask. Tag that person in the issue and assign the issue to them.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Inbox
Check your GitHub inbox for the request to review a colleague’s codelist. Open the request and follow the link to the issue or pull request.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Clone
Clone a repository to make a local copy on your computer. To make a copy in your GitHub account, fork the repository.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Branch
A branch is an independent line of development.

The default and main line of development is typically called the main branch.
Branches allow developers to work on new features or bug fixes in isolation without affecting the stable, main code.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Fork
A fork is a copy of a repository in your GitHub account. You can change your fork without changing the original, then propose your changes to the original project with a pull request. A fork is useful when you do not have write access to the original repository.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Pull Request (PR)
A pull request (PR) proposes changes from one branch to another, usually so the team can discuss and review them before merging.

PRs are where discussion, code review, and automated testing happen before the code is integrated.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text: Our first PR

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
YOUR TURN Complete your review

Clone your colleague’s repository if you have write access. If you do not, fork it and clone your fork.
Create a branch (for example, review_codelist).
Review the codelist and make the agreed changes.
Commit your changes.
Push your branch to GitHub.
Open a pull request targeting your colleague’s repository.
Link the pull request to the relevant issue.
Ask the colleague who assigned the review to review your pull request.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Merge
A merge integrates changes from one branch into another. Once a pull request is approved, a repository maintainer can merge it into the target branch.

Let’s merge your Pull Requests

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
YOUR TURN
Review the pull request in your repository. Approve it or request changes, then merge it once you and the author agree it is ready.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
How everything works
Git








Command
Description




git init
Create a new local repository.


git clone <url>
Copy a remote repository locally.


git remote add origin <url>
Add a new remote repository.


git status
Check status of changes and branch.


git add <file>
Stage specific file(s) for commit.


git commit -m "message"
Commit staged changes.


git log
View commit history.


git diff
Show unstaged changes.


git branch <name>
Create a new branch.


git checkout <branch>
Switch to a branch.


git merge <branch>
Merge another branch into the current one.


git fetch
Download updates from remote (no merge).


git pull
Fetch and merge changes from remote.


git push
Push local commits to remote.


git revert <commit>
Revert a specific commit with a new one.





GitHub Desktop provides a graphical interface for working with Git and GitHub.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text: Workflow

text: Update from main

text:
Update from main

Change to your_branch branch
Branch > Update from main
Push

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
.gitignore

The .gitignore file tells git which files or folders to skip when tracking changes. It prevents temporary, sensitive, or unnecessary files from being added to a repository. Common examples include log files, build artifacts, and environment files. This keeps the repo clean and focused on essential code and assets.

To ignore a file, add its name, for example my_file.txt.
To ignore a folder, add its name followed by a slash, for example folder/.
Use patterns such as *.txt to ignore all .txt files.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text: Merge conflicts

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text: Merge conflicts

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Merge conflicts
A merge conflict happens when Git cannot automatically combine overlapping changes. Conflicts can be resolved; they are a normal part of working together.

Keep pull requests focused and reasonably small.
Update your branch from main regularly, especially before opening a pull request.
If GitHub Desktop reports a conflict, review the conflicting changes and ask for help if you are unsure how to resolve them.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
section: Link a pull request to an issue
text:
Link a pull request to an issue
To link an issue and close it when the pull request is merged into the repository’s default branch, put one of these keywords followed by the issue number in the pull request description:

close #12 / closes #12
resolve #12 / resolves #12
fix #12 / fixes #12


To link an issue without using a closing keyword, link it manually from the Development section of the pull request sidebar.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Templates

Templates can be used to create new repositories:

text:
GitHub on the server
When working with the rstudio server, you won’t be able to access to GitHub Desktop, so the UI is going to be a bit more complicated.

First you will need to link your RStudio server with your github account, to do that you can follow this Tutorial.


Once done you will have to navigate trough the Git panel:

Delete the mock repo

title: OmopViewer
text:
From reports to apps
In Quarto we wrote a report and rendered it. With Shiny, we can let someone explore the results themselves: choose a database, change a filter, or switch between plots.
A Shiny app has two main parts:


UI (user interface): what you see, such as buttons, sliders, and spaces for plots.

Server: the R code that responds to inputs and creates the outputs.

Change an input and Shiny updates the outputs that depend on it. That is reactivity.

title: OmopViewer
text:
Your first Shiny app
Open your R Project. In RStudio, choose File → New File → Shiny Web App… and select a single-file app, app.R.
Click Run App and move the slider in the starter histogram example. What changes?

The next two slides show the UI and server for this example. Put them together in app.R.
The app keeps your R session busy while it runs. Click Stop in RStudio before running other code or restarting the app.

title: OmopViewer
text:
The UI: what goes where?

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Hello Shiny!"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("bins", "Number of bins:",
                  min = 1, max = 50, value = 30)
    ),
    mainPanel(plotOutput("distPlot"))
  )
)

bins is the slider’s ID. distPlot is the space where the server will put the plot. These IDs connect the two parts of the app.

title: OmopViewer
OmopViewer
section: Give the UI a style with bslib
text:
Give the UI a style with bslib
bslib gives us layouts, cards, sidebars, and themes. Replace the previous ui block with this one and keep the same server:

library(bslib)

ui <- page_sidebar(
  title = "My first app",
  theme = bs_theme(bootswatch = "flatly"),
  sidebar = sidebar(
    sliderInput("bins", "Number of bins:",
                min = 1, max = 50, value = 30)
  ),
  card(plotOutput("distPlot"))
)

Run shinyApp(ui, server) again. The layout changes, but the matching IDs mean the slider and plot still work together.

title: OmopViewer
text:
Meet OmopViewer
Building every filter, table, and plot by hand takes time. OmopViewer creates a Shiny app for us from supported OMOP study results.
It prepares the panels and code. We can then make small changes to fit our study.

Two ways to use it:


launchDynamicApp(): open a viewer and upload results to explore.

exportStaticApp(): create app files that we can inspect, edit, and share.

title: OmopViewer
text:
What data does it need?
OmopViewer works with summarised_result objects: summary estimates together with settings that describe the analyses that produced them.
The settings help OmopViewer choose the appropriate panels for supported result types.

For this exercise, we will use cohort attrition and characteristics results from the reporting training, for amoxicillin and metformin.
Download OmopViewer results for this exercise. The four-column Data 1 and Data 2 files from the Quarto session are ordinary tables and cannot be used directly here.

title: OmopViewer
text:
YOUR TURN Get the results

Open the course website’s Downloads tab and choose your GitHub username.
Click Download OmopViewer results.
Save omopviewer_results.csv in the data folder of your R Project.
Create an R script called omopviewer.R in your project. We will use it to explore and export an app.

The code in these slides is for you to run in RStudio. It does not launch an app when we render the presentation.

title: OmopViewer
text:
Open the dynamic viewer

library(OmopViewer)

launchDynamicApp()

Upload omopviewer_results.csv, then use Bind data and load shiny to build the panels.

This is a quick way to look at results without creating an app project. Stop the app in RStudio when you want to continue coding.

title: OmopViewer
text:
YOUR TURN Explore the results

Find the cohort characteristics and attrition panels.
Switch between amoxicillin and metformin. What changes?
Try a filter or a table option, then update the output if the panel has an update button.
Pick one result you would want to show in a report.

Think about the UI and server we just saw: which controls are inputs, and which tables or plots are outputs?

title: OmopViewer
text:
Import the results in R
Stop the dynamic app and return to omopviewer.R.

library(OmopViewer)
library(omopgenerics)
library(here)
library(shiny)

result <- importSummarisedResult(
  here("data", "omopviewer_results.csv")
)
settings(result)

Use importSummarisedResult() to restore the results and their settings. read_csv() alone does not reconstruct this object.

title: OmopViewer
section: Export an app we can edit
text:
Export an app we can edit

exportStaticApp(
  result = result,
  directory = here("viewer"),
  title = "My study results",
  background = TRUE,
  summary = TRUE,
  open = FALSE
)

runApp(here("viewer", "shiny"))

OmopViewer creates a shiny folder inside viewer. Here, “static” means the results are supplied when we generate the app; the app itself is still interactive and needs R to run.

title: OmopViewer
text:
What did OmopViewer create?
Stop the app, then open viewer/shiny in RStudio’s Files pane.






File
What to look for



global.R
Packages and data loaded for the app.


ui.R
Layout, panels, labels, and input controls.


server.R
Code that responds to inputs and builds outputs.


background.md
Text for the background panel.



rawData/ and data/

Original results, preparation code, and prepared app data.



Our first app had UI and server together in app.R. This app keeps them in separate files so they are easier to explore.

title: OmopViewer
text:
Start with the export options
Before editing the generated files, try changing the title and hiding the summary panel:

exportStaticApp(
  result = result,
  directory = here("viewer_custom"),
  title = "Exploring our cohorts",
  background = TRUE,
  summary = FALSE,
  open = FALSE
)

runApp(here("viewer_custom", "shiny"))

We use a second folder so we can compare the two apps. There are also options for themes, logos, and organising panels.

title: OmopViewer
text:
YOUR TURN Make it yours
Stop the app and work in viewer_custom/shiny:

Edit background.md: add a heading and two sentences explaining what someone can explore.
Open ui.R. Find a visible label and change its text. Keep input and output IDs the same so their connections still work.
Find the corresponding input or output in server.R. Can you follow what it does?
Run the app again and check your changes.


runApp(here("viewer_custom", "shiny"))

Save your edits before restarting. Exporting again to the same location can overwrite the generated app, so use a new folder if you want to keep your manual changes.

title: OmopViewer
text:
Final remarks


Shiny: the UI collects inputs and displays outputs; the server connects them with R code.

OmopViewer: creates the app structure and result panels for us.
Use the dynamic viewer to explore, or export an app when you want to customise it.

Start with a small change, run the app, and see what happens :)

title: OmopViewer
text:
Useful links

OmopViewer documentation

bslib layouts and themes

Adapted from the HDS reporting training.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
Why OmopStudyBuilder?
We have seen how an R Project keeps our work together and how GitHub helps us share it. Now imagine several teams running the same study in different OMOP databases.
It helps if everyone knows where to find the code, the instructions, and the results.

OmopStudyBuilder gives us a common starting structure for study projects and repositories. We add the study-specific code and documentation.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
What will we do?

Create the study structure with initStudy().
Explore the generated files and publish the repository on GitHub.
See how renv records the packages a project uses.
Use reviewStudy() to get an overview of the code and dependencies.

The package also has Docker tools for running studies in containers. Today we will focus on setting up and reviewing a study.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
Create a study
Install the package from CRAN if you do not have it yet:

install.packages("OmopStudyBuilder", dependencies = TRUE)

From your current R Project, choose a new folder beside it. Replace yourusername with your GitHub username:

library(OmopStudyBuilder)
library(here)

study_dir <- file.path(dirname(here()), "hds-study-yourusername")
initStudy(
  directory = study_dir,
  studyTitle = "My HDS practice study",
  studyLeads = "Your name",
  studyDescription = "Practising a shared OMOP study structure."
)

The destination must be new or empty. Let initStudy() create its contents before opening any of the generated R Projects.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
What did it create?
hds-study-yourusername/
├── README.md
├── INSTRUCTIONS.md
├── diagnosticsCode/
├── diagnosticsShiny/
├── studyCode/
└── studyShiny/


diagnosticsCode: prepare checks before the main analysis.

studyCode: define cohorts and run the study analyses.

diagnosticsShiny and studyShiny: places for apps that explore the results.

Both diagnostics and study default to TRUE. Set either to FALSE in initStudy() if you do not need that pair of folders.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
One repository, several R Projects
Each of the four component folders contains an .Rproj file. Open the project for the part you are working on.
For example, open studyCode/studyCode.Rproj for the main analysis. In that session, here() points to studyCode.







File or folder inside studyCode

What goes there?



codeToRun.R
The entry script, including database-specific settings.


runStudy.R
The sequence of study steps.



codelist/ and cohorts/

Code to define the study population.


analyses/
Code for the analyses.


Results/
Output from the study.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
YOUR TURN Explore the template

Run the initStudy() example with your own folder name and study details.
Read the root README.md and INSTRUCTIONS.md. Which parts would you update for a real study?
Open studyCode/studyCode.Rproj, then look at codeToRun.R and runStudy.R.
Find where you would add cohort definitions and an analysis.

For now, explore the scripts rather than sourcing them: the database connection and study-specific code are still to be filled in.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
section: YOUR TURN Put the study on GitHub
text:
YOUR TURN Put the study on GitHub
Use the whole study folder, hds-study-yourusername, as the repository root.

In GitHub Desktop, choose File → Add Local Repository… and select that folder.
If Desktop says it is not a Git repository, follow create a repository here. Use the existing folder and keep the README created by OmopStudyBuilder.
Review the files and commit any pending changes with a message such as Add study structure.
Click Publish repository, choose oxford-pharmacoepi as the organisation, and publish it as a private repository.
Open it on GitHub and check that the README and all four component folders are there.

Use a unique repository name. If you cannot select the organisation, ask the trainer to check your access.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
section: Keep the instructions with the code
text:
Keep the instructions with the code
In the root README, write a short description of your practice study. For example: which population would you study, and what would you measure?
Then use the workflow from the GitHub session:

Create a branch for your changes.
Commit and push them.
Open a pull request and ask a colleague whether the instructions are clear.

OmopStudyBuilder can also create a GitHub repository through initStudy() or linkGitHub() when R authentication is configured. See the CRAN reference manual for that route.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
Why use renv?
The same code can behave differently when people have different package versions. renv gives an R Project its own package library and records package versions in renv.lock.


The study developer prepares the environment and records it.
A colleague restores that environment when they run the study.
The lockfile is committed alongside the code, so changes can be reviewed in GitHub.

The generated study folders do not yet contain a lockfile. Prepare renv in each component R Project that you use, after deciding which packages its code needs.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
renv: the basic workflow
Open studyCode/studyCode.Rproj before setting up its environment. Install renv if needed, then initialise it once:

install.packages("renv")
library(renv)
init()

init() scans the project and prepares its package library and lockfile. It may need to install packages referenced by the template.






Function
When would we use it?



snapshot()
Record the package versions after changing and checking the code.


restore()
Install the versions recorded in an existing lockfile.


status()
Check whether the project library and lockfile agree.



Commit renv.lock and the activation files created by renv; its .gitignore excludes the local package library. renv records the R version but does not install R itself.
More detail: Introduction to renv.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
Get an overview with reviewStudy()
Before sharing code with a data partner, it is useful to see what is in the project.
From the studyCode R Project, install OmopStudyBuilder there if it is missing from your new renv library, then run:

library(OmopStudyBuilder)
library(here)

reviewStudy(dir = here(), dependencies = FALSE)

This prints a summary of the R scripts and JSON, CSV, and Excel files. We skip the dependency review here because the fresh template has no renv.lock yet.
It gives us a starting point for review; we still need to read the code and check that it answers the study question.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
Review the dependencies too
Once studyCode/renv.lock exists, run:

reviewStudy(dir = here(), type = "analysis")

By default, both code and dependencies are TRUE. The dependency review uses the lockfile and reports on package versions and sources.

For a reporting or app project, open that component’s R Project and use type = "reporting".
Run the review in the component folder containing the lockfile. A review of the repository root will not automatically review every component’s environment.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
YOUR TURN Review your study

Run reviewStudy(dir = here(), dependencies = FALSE) from studyCode.
Find the entry script and the analysis scripts in the output. Which are still empty?
If you have prepared a lockfile, run the dependency review too. Pick one package and find its recorded version.
Add a note to your pull request describing what still needs to be completed before the study can run.

Discuss the review with your colleague. A common folder structure makes it easier to find things, but the code and instructions still need a human review.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
Final remarks

Start with initStudy() so everyone recognises the study layout.
Keep the instructions and code together in GitHub.
Use renv to record and restore package versions.
Use reviewStudy() to help you inspect the project before sharing it.

Next, we will see how OmopViewer helps us build apps to explore study results.

title: OmopStudyBuilder
text:
Useful links

OmopStudyBuilder on CRAN
CRAN reference manual
Package guides and examples
Introduction to renv

Examples follow the CRAN release of OmopStudyBuilder, 0.1.1.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Quarto
Quarto is a free tool for creating documents from a plain-text source file. You can combine writing, code, and the results of that code in one place.
Use the same source to create reports, presentations, websites, and more. Quarto works with R, Python, Julia, and Observable.
In this training we will use R.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
What happens when you render?
You write your content in a .qmd file. When you render it, Quarto runs the code, adds its output to your writing, and creates the finished document.
That makes it easier to update a report when the data changes: update the data, render again, and the numbers and figures are refreshed from the code.

title: Introduction to Quarto
section: How to create a Quarto document
text:
How to create a Quarto document
Open the R Project you created earlier. In RStudio, choose File → New File → Quarto Document….
Give the document a name and save it inside your project. Keeping the document and its data together makes it easier to find and share your work.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text: Create a Quarto document

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Choose a format and render
Start with HTML and click Render. Quarto will create a document you can open in your browser.

Try rendering the same source as Word and PDF, then compare the results.
For the template exercise, switch the output format to Word.


The writing and code stay in the .qmd source. You can render it again whenever you update the content or data.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Parts of a Quarto document
A .qmd file has two main parts:


Metadata at the top, between lines containing ---. This is YAML and stores settings such as the title and output format.

Document body below the metadata. This contains your text, headings, code, and other content to render.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Write some text
Quarto uses Markdown for headings and basic formatting. For example:
# Main heading
## Smaller heading

This is a paragraph with **bold text**.

- This is a list item.
- And another one.

Render the document and see how the source becomes a formatted page.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Add some code
Put R code in a code chunk. Quarto can run it and include the result in the document:

scores <- c(7, 8, 10)
mean(scores)

[1] 8.333333



The code and its result are connected: change the values and render again to update the result.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
echo, eval, messages, and warnings

These options control what happens to code chunks:


echo: show (TRUE) or hide (FALSE) the code in the rendered document.

eval: run (TRUE) or skip (FALSE) the code.

message and warning: show or hide messages and warnings produced by the code.


Set options in the chunk header, or set document-wide defaults in the YAML under execute:. For example, a chunk with {r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE} runs summary(scores) but hides its code and messages while showing the result.


You can also change this options globaly with the initial block of yaml file, the following block for example will make all the code to be hidden but executed:
---
execute:
  echo: false
  eval: true
---

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
YOUR TURN

Open the course website’s Downloads tab and choose your GitHub username.
Click Download Data 1 results and save data1.csv in a data folder inside your R Project.
Read it into your Quarto document. Add a sentence, table, or plot that tells us something about the data.

title: Introduction to Quarto
section: YOUR TURN Read, summarise, and plot
text:
YOUR TURN Read, summarise, and plot
Read the CSV with readr, then find the row with the highest prevalence:

library(readr)
library(here)
library(dplyr)
data <- read_csv(here("data", "data1.csv"))
highest_example <- data |>
  filter(prevalence == max(prevalence))

In your document, you could write this sentence using inline R:
The highest prevalence is `r highest_example$prevalence`
for `r highest_example$condition`
in `r highest_example$database` in `r highest_example$year`.
For example, you could describe the highest value in a sentence, make a table, or plot prevalence by year and condition.
These chunks are examples for your own document.

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data, aes(x = year, y = prevalence, colour = condition)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~database)

Inline R expressions run when you render the document, just like code in a chunk.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Spacing in Quarto
Leave a blank line in the source to start a new paragraph. A single newline in the source may still appear as part of the same paragraph when rendered.
In a presentation, a new ## heading starts a new slide. Keep headings short so the audience can see the main point at a glance.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Use templates
A template gives documents a shared look and saves you from formatting every report by hand. For a Word report, a reference document can define headings, fonts, spacing, headers, footers, and caption styles.
Quarto uses the content and styles in your .qmd file; Word uses the matching styles in the reference document to decide how those parts look.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Example of a Word template
The darwinReportRef.docx template is an example of a Word reference document.
Download it and open it in Word to explore the styles. In your Quarto document, set it as the reference-doc for Word output, then render the report to apply those styles.
For example, save the template in your project folder and add this to the document YAML:
format:
  docx:
    reference-doc: "darwinReportRef.docx"

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Custom styles for captions
You can give a block of text a style name that exists in the Word reference document:
:::{custom-style="FigureCaption"}
Figure 1. The prevalence of the different condition over time.
:::

:::{custom-style="CaptionFooter"}
CI = confidence interval
:::
Create or change the FigureCaption and CaptionFooter styles in the Word template to control their appearance. The style names in the document and template need to match.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
YOUR TURN
A new data partner sends updated results at the last minute, and two other partners have updated their old results. No need to rebuild the report by hand:

In your username tab on Downloads, click Download Data 2 results and save data2.csv in your data folder.
Update your read_csv() line to read data2.csv.
Render the Quarto document again and compare the results.


The report is refreshed from the new data. Check what changed for SIDI Plata, notice the new SIDI Or results, and confirm that SIDI Bronze stayed the same.

title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
Final remarks

Keep the writing, code, and results together in the .qmd source.
Use a template when reports need a consistent look.
When the data changes, update the input files and render again.


That’s Quarto: write it once, render it when you need it, and let the code update the results.
